result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.k_edge_subgraphs()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the maximal k-edge-connected subgraphs of a graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L53706-L53769){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.k_edge_subgraphs(k) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![k-edge-connected subgraphs](/assets/graphs/k-edge-subgraphs.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Both sides show hubs u and v joined through a, b and c, with k = 3. Left: k_edge_components(3) counts paths through the whole graph, and the three edge-disjoint u–v paths (accent, teal, violet) put u and v in one component, with a, b and c alone. Right: k_edge_subgraphs(3) counts only edges inside each group, and u and v are not even adjacent, so every subgraph is a single node." width="100%"} A k-edge-connected subgraph is a set of nodes whose induced subgraph stays connected after removing any `k - 1` of its own edges. This method returns the maximal such sets, which partition the nodes. Unlike `k_edge_components()`, only edges inside the set count, so each group is robust on its own, which is what matters when, say, a cluster of servers must stay connected using only its internal links. Every node not in a larger group forms its own singleton. On a directed graph, each group must be strongly k-edge-connected on its own: `k` edge-disjoint paths run each way between any two members using only the group's edges. Parallel edges count separately and self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The required edge connectivity (at least 1). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node sets as sorted lists of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `k` is less than 1. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The k-edge-connected components of the graph are computed (see `k_edge_components()`), and then recursively the components of each one's induced subgraph, until every set is a single component of its own induced subgraph. Each set then has edge connectivity at least `k` (or is a single node), and maximality follows because the components of the whole graph contain every k-edge-connected subgraph. Results match NetworkX's `k_edge_subgraphs`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Hubs `u` and `v` are joined by three edge-disjoint paths through `a`, `b` and `c`, so they form a 3-edge-connected component. But those paths run through other nodes, and on their own `u` and `v` are not even adjacent, so every 3-edge-connected subgraph is a single node: ::: {#137edd1a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["u", "v", "a", "b", "c"]) g.add_edges([("u", "a"), ("a", "v"), ("u", "b"), ("b", "v"), ("u", "c"), ("c", "v")]) def show(groups): return [[g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in group] for group in groups] show(g.k_edge_components(3)), show(g.k_edge_subgraphs(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ([['u', 'v'], ['a'], ['b'], ['c']], [['u'], ['v'], ['a'], ['b'], ['c']]) ``` ::: :::
